stances.claim: The Philippine judiciary has suffered three sequential assaults on its independence under Marcos: (1) the 1972 mass-resignation requirement, (2) the 1973 Constitution's 'until 70 unless sooner replaced' authorization, and (3) the 1980 Judiciary Act's removal power -- a layered diminishment best understood as cumulative, not episodic.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-assaults framing (using numbered enumeration to make a structural argument)

stances.claim: Cory Aquino's post-Marcos purge plus the JBC's failure (purged judges returning, promotions requiring political backers) mean the 1987 Constitution's independence-restoration project never fully succeeded.

The Supreme Court has made SALNs of justices and judges difficult to obtain by imposing conditions not found in RA 3019 or RA 6713 -- although CJ interjects that on June 11 2013 the Court granted PCIJ access to all sitting justices' SALNs and PDS from appointment to 2011.
stances.rhetorical_move: criticism-with-corrective-interjection (CJ defends recent SC action while preserving Diokno's broader critique)

stances.claim: The immutability-of-final-judgments doctrine -- a time-honored principle -- has been institutionalized away by Section 3 of Rule 15 of the May 4 2010 SC Internal Rules, opening the door to second motions for reconsideration starting with the Sixteen Cities case.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-erosion narrative (locating a precise rule and a precise case as origin point)

stances.claim: Court congestion is severe (26 percent of courts judge-less) and compounded by US-imported procedures designed for jury systems that PH does not have -- Filipino procedures should reflect the Filipino concept of justice.

Chambers practice (decisions via old-boys networks, political connections, school chums, relatives, friends) requires disclosure mandates for justices/judges on clients and potential conflicts -- transparency is the corrective.

Despite these failures the judiciary remains capable of reform; Ka Pepe's 1981 amicus held that all generations of Filipino lawyers bear shared responsibility for the sorry state of the judiciary, and the struggle for justice must continue 'in time, yet under the aspect of eternity.'
stances.rhetorical_move: hope-without-illusion closing (shared-responsibility framing as motivational close)
stances.confidence: asserted via Diokno and Ka Pepe

notable_anecdotes: CJ's rare mid-column interjection -- correcting Diokno's SALN-difficulty claim by pointing to the June 11 2013 SC order granting PCIJ access to all sitting justices' SALNs and PDS from appointment to 2011 -- the column's only moment where CJ defends the institution he led against the lecturer's critique while still publishing the critique.

The statistic '26 percent of our courts -- more than one out of every four -- have no judges' -- the single most concrete metric in the column, used to bridge philosophical critique into operational reality.

Ka Pepe's 1981 amicus quote: 'we all must bear some share of responsibility... most of us by unnecessary delays... and all by not speaking out as often and as forcefully as we could' -- transposed into 2013 as still relevant; the patrilineal voice from De La Llana vs Alba carries the column's ethical weight.

Kazantzakis transposition closing: 'the superior virtue is not to receive justice, it is to fight relentlessly for it -- to struggle for justice in time, yet under the aspect of eternity' -- the freedom-to-justice substitution as the column's philosophical close.
Diokno's proposal that justices and judges disclose their clients and conflicts of interest -- the single most operationally specific institutional-design reform in the column.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban continues the Diokno lecture series by presenting the Dean's diagnosis: does the Philippine judiciary reflect the Filipino concept of justice articulated last Sunday? Diokno traces three Marcos-era assaults on judicial independence -- the 1972 forced resignation of all judges, the 1973 Constitution's 'until 70 unless sooner replaced' authorization, and the 1980 Judiciary Act's removal power -- followed by Cory Aquino's post-Marcos purge and the 1987 Constitution's JBC vetting that 'has not lived up to its intended purpose' as purged judges found their way back and promotion came to require political backers. Diokno laments that the Supreme Court made SALNs difficult to obtain by imposing conditions not in RA 3019 or RA 6713; Panganiban interjects that on June 11, 2013 the SC granted PCIJ access to all sitting justices' SALNs and PDS from appointment to 2011 -- a rare mid-column defense of his former institution. Diokno indicts the erosion of the immutability-of-final-judgments doctrine starting with the 'Sixteen Cities' case and institutionalized in Section 3 of Rule 15 of the May 4, 2010 SC Internal Rules allowing second motions for reconsideration. He cites court congestion (26 percent of courts have no judges), cumbersome US-imported procedures designed for jury systems PH does not have, and 'chambers practice' decided via old-boys networks, school chums, relatives and friends -- proposing mandatory disclosure of clients and potential conflicts. He closes with Ka Pepe Diokno's 1981 amicus in De La Llana vs Alba: 'we all must bear some share of responsibility... and all by not speaking out as often and as forcefully as we could' -- and Nikos Kazantzakis transposed: 'the superior virtue is not to receive justice, it is to fight relentlessly for it -- to struggle for justice in time, yet under the aspect of eternity.'
